vsm1.2:73.1: xiii. The sitter’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I refuse lying down”
vsm1.2:73.3: The sitter can get up in any one of three watches of the night and walk up and down: for lying down is the only posture not allowed.
vsm1.2:74.2: Herein, one who is strict is not allowed a back-rest or cloth band or binding-strap to prevent falling while asleep.
vsm1.2:74.3: The medium one is allowed any one of these three.
vsm1.2:74.4: The mild one is allowed a back-rest, a cloth band, a binding-strap, a cushion, a “five-limb” and a “seven-limb.”
vsm1.2:74.5: A “five-limb” is a chair made with four legs and a support for the back.
vsm1.2:74.6: A “seven-limb” is one made with four legs, a support for the back and an arm support on each side.
vsm1.2:74.7:
They made that, it seems, for the Elder Pīṭhābhaya (Abhaya of the Chair).
The elder became a non-returner, and then attained Nibbāna.
vsm1.2:74.8: As soon as any one of these three lies down, his ascetic practice is broken. This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:75.1:
The benefits are these. The mental shackle described thus, “He dwells indulging in the pleasure of lying prone,
the pleasure of lolling, the pleasure of torpor” (M I 102), is severed;
vsm1.2:75.2:
his state is suitable for devotion to any meditation subject; his deportment inspires confidence;
his state favours the application of energy; he develops the right practice.
vsm1.2:76.1:
The adept that can place crosswise
His feet to rest upon his thighs
And sit with back erect shall make
Foul Māra’s evil heart to quake.
vsm1.2:76.2:
No more in supine joys to plump
And wallow in lethargic dump;
Who sits for rest and finds it good
Shines forth in the Ascetics’ Wood.
vsm1.2:76.3:
The happiness and bliss it brings
Has naught to do with worldly things;
So must the sitter’s vow befit
The manners of a man of wit.
vsm1.2:76.4: This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades, breach, and benefits, in the case of the sitter’s practice.
vsm1.2:77.0: Miscellaneous Discussion of the Ascetic Practices
vsm1.2:77.1:
Now, there is the commentary according to the stanza:
(4) As to the profitable triad,
(5) “Ascetic” and so on distinguished,
(6) As to groups, and also (7) singly,
The exposition should be known (see §3).
vsm1.2:78.1:
4. Herein, as to the profitable triad: (Dhs, p.1) all the ascetic practices, that is to say, those of trainers,
ordinary men, and men whose cankers have been destroyed, may be either profitable
vsm1.2:78.2: or in the Arahant’s case indeterminate. No ascetic practice is unprofitable.
vsm1.2:78.3:
But if someone should say: There is also an unprofitable ascetic practice because of the words
“One of evil wishes, a prey to wishes, becomes a forest dweller” (A III 219), etc.,
vsm1.2:78.4: he should be told: We have not said that he does not live in the forest with unprofitable consciousness.
vsm1.2:78.5: Whoever has his dwelling in the forest is a forest dweller; and he may be one of evil wishes or of few wishes.
vsm1.2:78.6:
But, as it was said above (§11), they “are the practices (aṅga) of a bhikkhu who is ascetic (dhuta) because he has shaken off
(dhuta) defilement by undertaking one or other of them. Or the knowledge that has got the name “ascetic” (dhuta) because it
shakes off (dhunana) defilement is a practice (aṅga) belonging to these, thus they are “ascetic practices” (dhutaṅga).
vsm1.2:78.7:
Or alternatively, they are ascetic (dhuta) because they shake off (niddhunana) opposition, and they
are practices (aṅga) because they are a way (paṭipatti).”
vsm1.2:78.8:
Now, no one called “ascetic” on account of what is unprofitable could have these as his practices; nor does what is unprofitable
shake off anything so that those things to which it belonged as a practice could be called “ascetic practices.”
vsm1.2:78.9: And what is unprofitable does not both shake off cupidity for robes, etc., and become the practice of the way.
vsm1.2:78.10: Consequently it was rightly said that no ascetic practice is unprofitable.
vsm1.2:79.1: And those who hold that an ascetic practice is outside the profitable triad have no ascetic practice as regards meaning.
vsm1.2:79.2: Owing to the shaking off of what is non-existent could it be called an ascetic practice?
vsm1.2:79.3:
Also there are the words “Proceeded to undertake the ascetic qualities” (Vin III
15), and it follows that those words are contradicted.
vsm1.2:79.4: So that should not be accepted. This, in the first place, is the commentary on the profitable triad.
vsm1.2:80.1:
5. As to “ascetic and so on distinguished,” the following things should be understood, that is to say, ascetic,
a preacher of asceticism, ascetic states, ascetic practices, and for whom the cultivation of ascetic practices is suitable.
vsm1.2:81.1: Herein, ascetic means either a person whose defilements are shaken off, or a state that entails shaking off defilements.
vsm1.2:81.2: A preacher of asceticism: one is ascetic but not a preacher of asceticism, another is not ascetic but a preacher of asceticism,
vsm1.2:81.3: another is neither ascetic nor a preacher of asceticism, and another is both ascetic and a preacher of asceticism.
vsm1.2:82.1:
Herein, one who has shaken off his defilements with an ascetic practice but does not advise and instruct
another in an ascetic practice, like the Elder Bakkula, is “ascetic but not a preacher of asceticism,”
vsm1.2:82.2: according as it is said: “Now, the venerable Bakkula was ascetic but not a preacher of asceticism.”
vsm1.2:82.3:
One who has not shaken off his own defilements but only advises and instructs another in an ascetic practice,
like the Elder Upananda, is “not ascetic but a preacher of asceticism,”
vsm1.2:82.4: according as it is said: “Now, the venerable Upananda son of the Sakyans was not ascetic but a preacher of asceticism.”
vsm1.2:82.5: One who has failed in both, like Lāḷudāyin, is “neither ascetic nor a preacher of asceticism,”
vsm1.2:82.6: according as it is said: “Now, the venerable Lāḷudāyin was neither ascetic nor a preacher of asceticism.”
vsm1.2:82.7: One who has succeeded in both, like the General of the Dhamma, is “both ascetic and a preacher of asceticism,”
vsm1.2:82.8: according as it is said: “Now, the venerable Sāriputta was ascetic and a preacher of asceticism.”
vsm1.2:83.1:
Ascetic states: the five states that go with the volition of an ascetic practice, that is to say,
fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, and that specific quality
vsm1.2:83.2: are called “ascetic states’ because of the words “Depending on fewness of wishes” (A III 219), and so on.
vsm1.2:84.1: Herein, fewness of wishes and contentment are non-greed.
vsm1.2:84.2: Effacement and seclusion belong to the two states, non-greed and non-delusion. That specific quality is knowledge.
vsm1.2:84.3: Herein, by means of non-greed a man shakes off greed for things that are forbidden.
vsm1.2:84.4: By means of non-delusion he shakes off the delusion that hides the dangers in those same things.
vsm1.2:84.5:
And by means of non-greed he shakes off indulgence in pleasure due to sense desires
that occurs under the heading of using what is allowed.
vsm1.2:84.6:
And by means of non-delusion he shakes off indulgence in self-mortification that occurs under the heading of excessive
effacement in the ascetic practices. That is why these states should be understood as “ascetic states.”
vsm1.2:85.1:
Ascetic practices: these should be understood as the thirteen, that is to say,
the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice … the sitter’s practice,
vsm1.2:85.2: which have already been described as to meaning and as to characteristic, and so forth.
vsm1.2:86.1:
For whom the cultivation of ascetic practices is suitable: they are suitable for one of greedy
temperament and for one of deluded temperament.
vsm1.2:86.2: Why? Because the cultivation of ascetic practices is both a difficult progress and an abiding in effacement;
vsm1.2:86.3: and greed subsides with the difficult progress, while delusion is got rid of in those diligent by effacement.
vsm1.2:86.4:
Or the cultivation of the forest-dweller’s practice and the tree-root-dweller’s
practice here are suitable for one of hating temperament;
vsm1.2:86.5:
for hate too subsides in one who dwells there without coming into conflict.
This is the commentary “as to ‘ascetic’ and so on distinguished.”
vsm1.2:87.1:
6. and 7. As to groups and also singly. Now, 6. as to groups: these ascetic practices
are in fact only eight, that is to say, three principal
vsm1.2:87.3: Herein, the three, namely, the house-to-house-seeker’s practice, the one-sessioner’s practice,
vsm1.2:87.4: and the open-air-dweller’s practice, are principal practices.
vsm1.2:87.5: For one who keeps the house-to-house-seeker’s practice will keep the alms-food-eater’s practice;
vsm1.2:87.6:
and the bowl-food-eater’s practice and the later-food-refuser’s practice will be well
kept by one who keeps the one-sessioner’s practice.
vsm1.2:87.7:
And what need has one who keeps the open-air-dweller’s practice to keep
the tree-root-dweller’s practice or the any-bed-user’s practice?
vsm1.2:87.8: So there are these three principal practices that,
vsm1.2:87.9:
together with the five individual practices, that is to say, the forest-dweller’s practice, the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice,
the triple-robe-wearer’s practice, the sitter’s practice, and the charnel-ground-dweller’s practice, come to eight only.
vsm1.2:88.1:
Again they come to four, that is to say, two connected with robes, five connected with alms food,
five connected with the resting place, and one connected with energy.
vsm1.2:88.2: Herein, it is the sitter’s practice that is connected with energy; the rest are obvious.
vsm1.2:88.3: Again they all amount to two only, since twelve are dependent on requisites and one on energy.
vsm1.2:88.4: Also they are two according to what is and what is not to be cultivated.
vsm1.2:88.5:
For when one cultivating an ascetic practice finds that his meditation subject improves, he should cultivate it; but when
he is cultivating one and finds that his meditation subject deteriorates, he should not cultivate it.
vsm1.2:88.6: But when he finds that, whether he cultivates one or not, his meditation subject only improves and does not deteriorate,
vsm1.2:88.7:
he should cultivate them out of compassion for later generations. And when he finds that, whether he cultivates
them or not, his meditation subject does not improve, he should still cultivate them for the sake of acquiring
the habit for the future. So they are of two kinds as what is and what is not to be cultivated.
vsm1.2:89.1: And all are of one kind as volition.
vsm1.2:89.2:
For there is only one ascetic practice, namely, that consisting in the volition of undertaking.
Also it is said in the Commentary: “It is the volition that is the ascetic practice, they say.”
vsm1.2:90.1: 7. Singly: with thirteen for bhikkhus, eight for bhikkhunīs,
vsm1.2:90.2:
twelve for novices, seven for female probationers and female novices, and two for male and female
lay followers, there are thus forty-two.
vsm1.2:91.1: If there is a charnel ground in the open that complies with the forest-dweller’s practice,
vsm1.2:91.2: one bhikkhu is able to put all the ascetic practices into effect simultaneously.
vsm1.2:91.3:
But the two, namely, the forest-dweller’s practice and the later-food-refuser’s practice,
are forbidden to bhikkhunīs by training precept.
vsm1.2:91.4:
And it is hard for them to observe the three, namely, the open-air-dweller’s practice,
the tree-root-dweller’s practice, and the charnel-ground-dweller’s practice,
vsm1.2:91.5: because a bhikkhunī is not allowed to live without a companion,
vsm1.2:91.6:
and it is hard to find a female companion with like desire for such a place, and even if available, she would not escape
having to live in company. This being so, the purpose of cultivating the ascetic practice would scarcely be served.
vsm1.2:91.7:
It is because they are reduced by five owing to this inability to make use of certain of them
that they are to be understood as eight only for bhikkhunīs.
vsm1.2:92.1: Except for the triple-robe-wearer’s practice all the other twelve as stated should be understood to be for novices,
vsm1.2:92.2: and all the other seven for female probationers and female novices.
vsm1.2:92.3: The two, namely, the one-sessioner’s practice and the bowl-food-eater’s practice,
vsm1.2:92.4:
are proper for male and female lay followers to employ. In this way there are two ascetic practices.
This is the commentary “as to groups and also singly.”
vsm1.2:93.1:
And this is the end of the treatise on the ascetic practices to be undertaken for the purpose of perfecting
those special qualities of fewness of wishes, contentment, etc., by means of which there comes
about the cleansing of virtue as described in the Path of Purification,
vsm1.2:93.2:
which is shown under the three headings of virtue, concentration, and understanding,
contained in the stanza, “When a wise man, established well in virtue” (I.1).
vsm1.2:93.3:
The second chapter called “The Description of the Ascetic Practices” in the Path of Purification
composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.
